analysis.one_liner: Requires federal background checks and recordkeeping for ammunition sales and bans certain armor-piercing and incendiary bullets.
analysis.headline: The ammunition background check bill drew a Democratic sponsor and 5 Democratic cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing, and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the same instant background check used for gun sales before someone could buy ammunition, and would have required private ammunition transfers to go through a licensed dealer. It also imposed recordkeeping and bulk-sale reporting on ammunition dealers and banned the transfer of Teflon-coated armor-piercing and incendiary ammunition, while letting people keep whatever they already lawfully owned. It never received a vote in committee or on the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would gain the most, under the bill's own logic: federal law already makes it illegal to sell ammunition to felons, fugitives, drug addicts, and certain others, but no seller has ever been required to check, so a prohibited buyer can walk in and buy ammunition with no questions asked. The bill would close that gap using the existing instant check system, which the bill's findings say completes most checks in about 30 seconds. Police would also gain a new paper trail: dealers would have to report large ammunition sales and significant thefts or losses to law enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence; police

how_it_helps.text: Closes a gap in the law: ammunition sales to prohibited buyers (felons, fugitives, drug addicts, and others) are already illegal, but sellers are never required to verify eligibility, unlike gun sales, which require an instant background check.

Uses the existing National Instant Criminal Background Check System, which the bill's findings say handles the vast majority of checks in about 30 seconds, and destroys the check records within three business days, so no purchase registry is created.
Requires dealers to report large ammunition sales and significant thefts or losses of ammunition to state and local police, giving investigators leads they currently do not get.

Bans the manufacture, transfer, and possession of Teflon-coated and incendiary bullets, while grandfathering ammunition lawfully owned on the day of enactment — though even grandfathered rounds could not be sold or transferred.

analysis.who_pays: Ammunition buyers would pay in time and hassle: a background check call and a photo ID for every purchase, with a default three-business-day wait if the system is slow. Licensed dealers would bear the heaviest compliance load — new recordkeeping, multiple-sale and theft reports, civil fines up to $100,000 for repeat knowing violations, and possible license suspension or revocation. Manufacturers and importers would face extended recordkeeping and restrictions, and anyone owning Teflon-coated or incendiary rounds could keep them but could never sell or transfer them, wiping out their resale value. Private individuals transferring ammunition without a dealer-run check would face fines and up to a year in jail.

drawbacks.text: Every ammunition purchase would require a federal check call and photo ID. The bill's own rural-dealer exception is narrow — it applies only where there are extremely few police per square mile, the dealer is extremely remote, and there are no telecommunications facilities — so most dealers get no relief from the added cost and delay.

The bill leaves key thresholds to the Attorney General's discretion: the 'large quantity' of ammunition that triggers a police report would be whatever the Attorney General decides indicates criminal intent, adjustable by region, and 'significant quantity' for theft reporting would be defined by regulation after enactment. Ordinary bulk purchases, like cases of target rounds, could easily be swept in.
People who lawfully owned Teflon-coated or incendiary ammunition could keep it but could never sell, give away, or transfer it — a confiscation of the item's value without compensation.

Private ammunition transfers between individuals would become federal crimes — fines and up to one year in imprisonment — unless the parties routed the transfer through a licensed dealer, and dealers would face escalating civil fines of $5,000, $25,000, and $100,000 for knowing violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a modest extension of a system that already works for gun sales: a quick check, no permanent records, and police notifications for bulk sales and thefts. The benefits — keeping ammunition from buyers who are already barred by law — are real but depend entirely on how many prohibited buyers the check actually stops. The costs are unevenly distributed: small dealers absorb most of the compliance burden, buyers with slow checks face the default three-business-day wait, and owners of grandfathered specialty ammunition lose the ability to ever transfer it. The open-ended quantities the Attorney General would define for bulk-sale reporting are the loosest part of the design and could burden ordinary volume purchasers. On balance the bill is a moderate restriction with moderate costs, not a sweeping one — but it was never debated or amended, so none of these design questions got aired.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and sat there until the Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on January 29, 2013, with Senators Chris Murphy and Frank Lautenberg as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
On February 12, 2013, a Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on the bill — the only substantive action it ever received.
The committee never voted the bill out, the Senate never debated it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ammunition retailers and manufacturers are better off: none of the background check, recordkeeping, reporting, or specialty-ammo restrictions ever took effect, and buyers continued purchasing ammunition with no check at all.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a subcommittee hearing in the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Five Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other action on it is recorded.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote; after one subcommittee hearing the bill received no further action of any kind.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 2013 Senate push to expand background checks, including to ammunition, during the post-Sandy Hook gun debate.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a committee or floor vote, no roll call ever recorded where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: Dealers would have to run a background check and verify photo ID on every ammunition sale, keep records, report bulk sales and thefts to police, and face fines up to $100,000 plus license suspension or revocation for knowing violations. Only a narrow class of extremely remote rural dealers is exempted, so the compliance burden falls on the whole retail trade.

The bill extends gun-style recordkeeping and interstate-sale restrictions to ammunition, requires reporting of production and disposition records, and bans manufacturing Teflon-coated armor-piercing and incendiary bullets outright.

Every purchaser would face a check and an ID requirement, private transfers would have to go through a licensed dealer, and owners of Teflon-coated or incendiary rounds could keep them but never transfer them. Buyers who pass the check — the overwhelming majority — face only delay and paperwork.
